t: The Category of Each Member in the Store — Conversion-Rate Bucketing in SQL
o: Three tables: Members (one row per member), Visits (who visited, when) and Purchases (which visit produced a charge). A member's conversion rate is 100 x (#purchases) / (#visits), and the tier is Diamond at rate >= 80, Gold for [50, 80), Silver below 50, and Bronze for members who never visited at all. Walking Example 1: Narihan has no visits, so Bronze. Winston visited once without buying: 100 x 0 / 1 = 0, Silver. Hercy converted his only visit: 100, Diamond. Alice bought on 1 of 2 visits: exactly 50, Gold. Bob bought once in 3 visits: 33.33, Silver. Two structural requirements drive the query: members without visits must survive aggregation (LEFT JOIN, not INNER JOIN), and both counts must come out of one grouped join — COUNT(visit rows) versus COUNT(non-null purchase values) exploits that COUNT ignores NULLs.
k: Conversion rate = ROUND(100 * purchases / visits); bucket it with an ordered CASE at 80 and 50.
COUNT(v.visit_id) counts visits while COUNT(p.charged_amount) counts purchases from the same joined rows — unmatched LEFT JOIN rows contribute NULLs that COUNT skips.
Members who never visited must still appear as Bronze, so chain LEFT JOINs from Members rather than filtering with inner joins.

a.n: Approach 1: One Grouped Join Chain with CASE
a.i: Join Members to Visits to Purchases, group by member, and compute both counts over the joined rows in a single pass. The tier falls out of an ordered CASE evaluated on the rounded percentage, with a zero-visit branch first.
s: LEFT JOIN Visits v ON m.member_id = v.member_id.
LEFT JOIN Purchases p ON v.visit_id = p.visit_id.
Compute visits = COUNT(v.visit_id) and buys = COUNT(p.charged_amount).
Emit Bronze when visits = 0, else bucket ROUND(100 * buys / visits) via CASE.

c.python:
-- Database problem: submit this MySQL query.
SELECT m.member_id,
       m.name,
       CASE
           WHEN COUNT(v.visit_id) = 0 THEN 'Bronze'
           WHEN ROUND(100 * COUNT(p.charged_amount) / COUNT(v.visit_id)) >= 80 THEN 'Diamond'
           WHEN ROUND(100 * COUNT(p.charged_amount) / COUNT(v.visit_id)) >= 50 THEN 'Gold'
           ELSE 'Silver'
       END AS category
FROM Members m
LEFT JOIN Visits v ON m.member_id = v.member_id
LEFT JOIN Purchases p ON v.visit_id = p.visit_id
GROUP BY m.member_id, m.name;

a.t: O(V + P + M log M) — each visit and purchase row is touched once during the join; grouping costs about linear time with hashing.
a.sp: O(M) — one grouped row per member.

a.i: Separate concerns: first reduce (Visits LEFT JOIN Purchases) to one row per member carrying its two counts, then attach those stats to every Member row with another LEFT JOIN. Members absent from the stats CTE are exactly the never-visitors and map straight to Bronze.
s: Build stats: group Visits LEFT JOIN Purchases by member_id, counting visits and purchases.
LEFT JOIN Members against stats on member_id.
Bucket ROUND(100 * buys / visits) with CASE for the remaining members.

c.python:
-- Database problem: submit this MySQL query.
WITH stats AS (
    SELECT v.member_id,
           COUNT(v.visit_id) AS visits,
           COUNT(p.charged_amount) AS buys
    FROM Visits v
    LEFT JOIN Purchases p ON v.visit_id = p.visit_id
    GROUP BY v.member_id
)
SELECT m.member_id,
       m.name,
       CASE
           WHEN s.visits IS NULL THEN 'Bronze'
           WHEN ROUND(100 * s.buys / s.visits) >= 80 THEN 'Diamond'
           WHEN ROUND(100 * s.buys / s.visits) >= 50 THEN 'Gold'
           ELSE 'Silver'
       END AS category
FROM Members m
LEFT JOIN stats s ON s.member_id = m.member_id;

a.t: O(V + P + M log M) — same asymptotics as Approach 1, but the aggregation touches fewer, narrower rows.
a.sp: O(M) — the CTE materializes one row per visiting member.

w: Either formulation passes easily at these sizes; prefer Approach 2 for readability once logic grows beyond simple bucketing. Pitfalls: using INNER JOIN anywhere silently deletes Narihan-style members (wrong Bronze rows); forgetting that MySQL's / performs decimal division is harmless here but matters if you compare unrounded fractions near boundaries — the statement's tiers apply to the ROUNDED rate; also include name in GROUP BY for strict ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY modes. Edge cases: a visit whose purchase row is missing entirely, members with visits but zero purchases (rate 0, Silver), and rates landing exactly on 50 or 80. Follow-up: return the raw conversion_rate column too — just add ROUND(100 * buys / visits, 2) to the select list.
